78\begin{center}
79{\it Dedicated to the memory of Xiao-Song Lin}
80\end{center}
81\begin{abstract}
82A cohomology theory for multiplications and comultiplications of Frobenius
83algebras is developed
84in
85low dimensions
86in analogy with Hochschild cohomology of
87bialgebras
88based on
89deformation theory.
90Concrete computations are provided for key examples.
91Skein theoretic constructions give rise to solutions to the
92Yang-Baxter equation
93using multiplications and comultiplications of Frobenius
94algebras, and $2$-cocycles are used to obtain deformations
95of $R$-matrices thus obtained.
96\end{abstract}
97\section{Introduction}
98Frobenius algebras are interesting to topologists as well as
99algebraists
100for
101numerous reasons including the following.
102First,
103$2$-dimensional topological quantum field theories are formulated
104in terms of commutative Frobenius
105algebras
106(see \cite{Kock}).
107Second, a Frobenius algebra structure exists on any
108finite-dimensional Hopf algebra with a left integral defined in the dual space.
109These
110Hopf algebras have found applications in topology through
111Kuperberg's invariant
112\cite{Kup91,Kup96},
113the Henning invariant \cite{KR95,Oht},
114and the theory of quantum groups from which the post-Jones invariants arise.
115Third, there is a $2$-dimensional Frobenius algebra that underlies Khovanov's cohomology theory~\cite{Kh}. See also~\cite{AF}.
116Our interest herein is to extend the cohomology theories defined in \cite{CCES1,CCES2} to Frobenius algebras and thereby construct new solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation (YBE). We expect that there are connections among these cohomology theories that extend beyond their formal definitions. Furthermore, we anticipate topological, categorical, and/or physical applications because of the diagrammatic nature of the theory.
117The $2$-cocycle conditions of Hochschild cohomology of algebras
118and
119bialgebras can be interpreted
120via deformations of algebras~\cite{GS}.
121In other words, a map
122satisfying the associativity condition can be deformed to obtain a
123new associative map in a larger vector space using $2$-cocycles.
124The same interpretation can be applied to quandle cohomology
125theory~\cite{CJKLS,CENS,CES}.
126A quandle is a set
127equipped with a self-distributive binary
128operation
129satisfying a few additional conditions
130that correspond to the properties
131that conjugation in a group enjoys.
132Quandles have been used in
133knot theory extensively (see \cite{CJKLS} and references therein
134for more aspects of quandles). Quandles and related structures
135can be used to
136construct
137set-theoretic solutions
138(called $R$-matrices)
139to the Yang-Baxter
140equation (see, for example, \cite{K&P} and its references).
141{}From this point of view, combined with the deformation $2$-cocycle interpretation, a quandle $2$-cocycle can be regarded as giving a cocycle deformation of an $R$-matrix.
142Thus
143we extend this idea to other algebraic constructions of $R$-matrices and construct new $R$-matrices from old via $2$-cocycle deformations.
144In \cite{CCES1,CCES2}, new $R$-matrices were constructed via $2$-cocycle deformations in two other algebraic contexts.
145Specifically,
146in \cite{CCES1}, self-distributivity was revisited from
147the point of
148view of coalgebra categories, thereby unifying Lie algebras and
149quandles in these categories. Cohomology theories of Lie algebras
150and quandles were given
151via a single
152definition,
153and deformations of
154$R$-matrices were constructed. In \cite{CCES2}, the adjoint map of
155Hopf algebras,
156which
157corresponds to the group conjugation map,
158was studied from the same viewpoint.
159A cohomology theory was
160constructed based on equalities satisfied by the adjoint map that are sufficient for
161it to satisfy the YBE.
162In this paper, we present an analog for Frobenius algebras according to the following organization. After a brief review of necessary materials in Section~\ref{prelimsec},
163a cohomology theory for Frobenius algebras is constructed in Section~\ref{cohsec}
164via deformation theory.
165Then Yang-Baxter solutions
166are constructed by skein methods in Section~\ref{YBEsec},
167followed by
168deformations of $R$-matrices by
169$2$-cocycles.
170The reader should be aware
171that the composition of the maps is
172read in the standard way from right to left $(gf)(x)=g(f(x))$ in
173text and from bottom to top in the diagrams. In this way, when
174reading from left to right one can draw from top to bottom and
175when reading a diagram from top to bottom, one can display the
176maps from left to right. The argument of a function (or input
177object from a category) is found at the bottom of the diagram.
178\section{Preliminaries} \label{prelimsec}
179A {\it Frobenius algebra} is an (associative) algebra (with
180multiplication $\mu: A \otimes A \rightarrow A$ and unit $\eta: k
181\rightarrow A$) over a field $k$ with a nondegenerate associative
182pairing $\beta: A \otimes A \rightarrow k$. Throughout
183this paper all algebras are
184finite-dimensional unless
185specifically
186stated otherwise. The pairing $\beta$ is also expressed by
187$\langle x|y\rangle=\beta(x \otimes y)$ for $x, y \in A$, and it
188is {\it associative}
189in the sense that
190$\langle xy | z\rangle=\langle x|y
191z\rangle$ for any $x,y,z \in A$.
192\begin{figure}[htb]
193\begin{center}
194\includegraphics[width=4.5in]{frodiag}
195\end{center}
196\caption{Diagrams for Frobenius algebra maps}
197\label{frodiag}
198\end{figure}
199A Frobenius algebra $A$ has a linear functional $\epsilon: A
200\rightarrow k$,
201called the {\it Frobenius form},
202such that the kernel
203contains no nontrivial left ideal.
204It is defined from $\beta$ by $\epsilon(x)=\beta(x \otimes 1)$,
205and conversely, a Frobenius form gives rise to a nondegenerate
206associative pairing $\beta$ by $\beta(x \otimes y)=\epsilon(xy)$,
207for $x, y \in A$.
208A Frobenius form has a unique copairing
209$\gamma: k \rightarrow A \otimes A$
210characterized by
211$$ (\beta \otimes |)(| \otimes \gamma) = |
212= (| \otimes \beta)(\gamma \otimes |) , $$
213where $|$ denotes the identity homomorphism on the algebra. We call this relation the
214{\it cancelation} of $\beta $ and $\gamma$.
215See the middle entry in the bottom row of Fig.~\ref{froaxioms}.
216This notation will distinguish this function from the identity element $1=1_A=\eta(1_k)$
217of the algebra that is the image of the identity of the ground field.
218A Frobenius algebra $A$ determines a coalgebra structure with
219$A$-linear (coassociative) comultiplication and the counit
220defined using the Frobenius form. The comultiplication $\Delta: A
221\rightarrow A \otimes A$ is defined by
222\begin{eqnarray*}
223\Delta &=& (\mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \gamma) \\
224&=& (| \otimes \mu)(\gamma \otimes |).
225\end{eqnarray*}
226The multiplication and comultiplication
227satisfy the following equality:
228$$ \Delta \mu = (\mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \Delta )=(| \otimes \mu)(\Delta \otimes |)$$
229which we call the {\it Frobenius compatibility condition}.
230\begin{figure}[htb]
231\begin{center}
232\includegraphics[width=4in]{froaxioms}
233\end{center}
234\caption{Equalities among Frobenius algebra maps }
235\label{froaxioms}
236\end{figure}
237A Frobenius algebra is {\it symmetric} if the pairing is
238symmetric,
239meaning that $\beta(x \otimes y)=\beta(y \otimes x)$ for any $x, y
240\in A$. A Frobenius algebra is {\it commutative} if it is commutative as
241an algebra. It is known (\cite{Kock} Prop.
2422.3.29) that a Frobenius algebra is commutative
243if and only if
244it is cocommutative as a coalgebra.
245The map $\mu \Delta $ of a Frobenius algebra
246is called the
247{\it handle operator,} and
248corresponds to multiplication by a central element called the {\it handle element}
249$\delta_h =\mu \gamma (1) $ (\cite{Kock}, page 128).
250Any semisimple Hopf algebra gives rise to
251a Frobenius algebra structure (see, for example, \cite{Kock}, page $135$).
252Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra
253with multiplication $\mu$ and unit $\eta$.
254Then $H$ is semisimple
255if and only if
256the bilinear form
257$\beta_{a\; b}=\sum \mu_{c\; d}^d \ \mu_{a\; b}^c $ is nondegenerate.
258If $H$ is semisimple,
259then
260the above defined $\beta$ gives rise to a Frobenius pairing.
261In this case the Frobenius form (a counit of the Frobenius algebra structure)
262is defined by $\epsilon_a=\sum \mu_{c\; d}^d =T$,
263the trace of $H$.
264This counit and the induced comultiplication of the resulting Frobenius algebra
265structure should not be confused with the counit and the comultiplication
266of the original Hopf algebra.
267We thank Y. Sommerhausser for explaining these relationships to us.
268We compute cohomology groups and the Yang-Baxter solutions
269for a variety of examples,
270and we review these
271mostly from \cite{Kock}.
272{}From the point of view of TQFTs, the value $\epsilon \eta (1)$ corresponds to a sphere
273$S^2$, $\delta_0 = \beta \gamma (1)$ to a torus $T^2$,
274and $\mu \Delta $ to adding an extra $1$-handle to a tube, so we
275will compute these values and maps.
276\begin{example}{\bf Complex numbers with trigonometric comultiplication.}\label{cplxex}
277{\rm
278Let $A=\C$ over $k=\R$ and
279let the basis be denoted by $1$ and $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Then the
280Frobenius form $\epsilon$ defined by
281$\epsilon(1)=1$ and
282$\epsilon(i)=0$ gives rise to the comultiplication $\Delta$,
283which is Sweedler's trigonometric coalgebra
284with
285$\Delta(1)=1 \otimes 1 - i \otimes i $, and
286$\Delta(i)=i \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes i $.
287We compute $\epsilon \eta (1) = 1$,
288$\mu \Delta (1)=2 \eta(1) $,
289and $\mu \Delta (i)=2i \eta(1) $
290so that $\mu \Delta $ is
291multiplication by $2$, which is the handle element $\delta_h$.
292We also have $\delta_0=2$. } \end{example}
293\begin{example}{\bf Polynomial algebras.\/}\label{polyex} {\rm
294Polynomial rings $k[x]/(x^n)$ over a field $k$ where $n$ is a positive
295integer are Frobenius
296algebras. In particular, for $n=2$, the algebra $A=k[x]/(x^2)$ was
297used in the Khovanov homology of knots~\cite{Kh}. For
298$A=k[x]/(x^2)$,
299the Frobenius form $\epsilon: A \rightarrow k$ is
300defined by $\epsilon(x)=1$ and $\epsilon(1)=0$.
301This induces the comultiplication
302$\Delta: A \rightarrow A \otimes A$ determined by
303$\Delta(1)=1 \otimes x + x \otimes 1$ and
304$\Delta(x)= x \otimes x $. The handle element is $\delta_h=2x$.
305More generally for $A=k[x]/(x^n)$
306and $\epsilon(x^{j})=1$ for $j=n-1$ and $0$ otherwise,
307the
308comultiplication is determined by $\Delta(1) =
309\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} x^i \otimes x^{n-1-i}$.
310We have
311$\mu \Delta (1) = n x^{n-1} $ and
312the handle element is $\delta_h=n x^{n-1} $.
313} \end{example}
314\begin{example}{\bf Group algebras.\/}\label{gpex} {\rm
315The group algebra $A=kG$ for a finite group $G$ over a field $k$
316is
317a Frobenius algebra with $\epsilon (x)=0$ for any $G \ni x \neq 1$
318and $\epsilon (1)=1$, where $1$ is identified with the identity
319element. The induced comultiplication is given by $\Delta(x)=\sum_{yz=x} y
320\otimes z$.
321One computes $\epsilon \eta (1) = 1$ and $\mu \Delta (x)=|G|x $,
322where $|G|$ is the order of $G$. In particular, note that $\mu
323\Delta = \delta_1 \id$ (recall that $\id$ denotes the identity map), where $\delta_1=|G|$ (the order of the group $G$), and $(\mu \Delta )^n =
324\delta_1^n \id$ for any $n \in \N$,
325so that the handle element is $\delta_h=\delta_1=|G|$, and
326$\delta_0=|G|$.
327There are other Frobenius forms
328on the group algebra A (again from \cite{Kock}). For example, for
329$A=kG$ where $G$ is the symmetric group on three letters,
330$A=k\langle x, y\rangle / (x^2-1, y^2-1, xyx=yxy )$, and
331$\epsilon(xyx)=1$ and otherwise zero, is a Frobenius form and the
332handle element is $2(xyx+x+y)$. } \end{example}
333\begin{example}{\bf $q$-Commutative polynomials.\/}\label{qpolyex} {\rm
334Let $X= k \langle x, y \rangle /(x^2, y^2, yx - q xy) $
335where $q=- A^{-2}$ for $A \in k$ with
336polynomial multiplication and $\epsilon(xy)=iA$,
337and zero for other basis elements.
338Then
339$$ \gamma(1)( =\Delta\eta (1)) = iA (x \otimes y) - i A^{-1} (y \otimes x)
340- i A^{-1} (xy \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes xy ) .$$
341One computes
342\begin{eqnarray*}
343\Delta(x) &=& - iA^{-1} (x \otimes xy + xy \otimes x) , \\
344\Delta(y) &=& - iA^{-1} (y \otimes xy + xy \otimes y) , \\
345\Delta(xy) &=& - iA^{-1} (xy \otimes xy) .
346\end{eqnarray*}
347The handle element is $\delta_h = iA^{-1} (A - A^{-1} )^2 (xy) $.
348} \end{example}
349\section{Deformations and cohomology groups}\label{cohsec}
350We describe the deformation theory of multiplication and
351comultiplication for Frobenius algebras mimicking \cite{GS},
352\cite{MrSt}, and our approach in \cite{CCES1,CCES2}. This approach
353will yield the definition of $2$-cocycles. We will define the
354chain complex for Frobenius algebras with chain groups in low
355dimensions \cite{GS, MrSt}. We expect topological applications in low dimensions.
356The differentials are defined via diagrammatically defined
357identities among relations.
358\subsection{Deformations}\label{deformsec}
359In \cite{MrSt},
360deformations of bialgebras were described.
361We follow that formalism and
362give deformations of multiplications and comultiplications of Frobenius algebras.
363A deformation of $A=(V, \mu, \Delta) $ is a
364$k[[t]]$-Frobenius algebra $A_t=(V_t, \mu_t, \Delta_t)$, where
365$V_t=V \otimes k[[ t ]]$ and
366$ V_t/(tV_t) \cong V$.
367Deformations
368of $\mu$ and $\Delta$ are given by $\mu_t= \mu + t \mu_1 + \cdots
369+ t^n \mu_n + \cdots : V_t \otimes V_t \rightarrow V_t$ and
370$\Delta_t = \Delta + t \Delta_1 + \cdots + t^n \Delta_n + \cdots :
371V_t \rightarrow V_t \otimes V_t$ where $\mu_i: V \otimes V
372\rightarrow V $, $\Delta_i : V \rightarrow V \otimes V$, $i=1, 2,
373\cdots$, are sequences of maps. Suppose $\bar{\mu}=\mu + \cdots +
374t^n \mu_n$ and $\bar{\Delta} =\Delta + \cdots + t^n \Delta_n$
375satisfy the
376Frobenius
377conditions (associativity, compatibility,
378and coassociativity) mod $t^{n+1}$, and suppose that there exist
379$\mu_{n+1}: V \otimes V \rightarrow V$ and $\Delta_{n+1}: V
380\rightarrow V \otimes V$ such that $\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1} \mu_{n+1}$
381and $\bar{\Delta}+ t^{n+1} \Delta_{n+1}$ satisfy the Frobenius
382algebra conditions mod $t^{n+2}$. Define $\xi_1 \in
383\Hom(V^{\otimes 3}, V)$, $\xi_2, \xi_2' \in \Hom(V^{\otimes 2}, V^{\otimes
3842})$, and $\xi_3 \in \Hom(V, V^{\otimes 3})$ by:
385\begin{eqnarray*}
386\bar{\mu} (\bar{\mu} \otimes |) - \bar{\mu}(| \otimes \bar{\mu})
387&=& t^{n+1}\xi_1
388\quad {\rm mod}\ t^{n+2} , \label{hoch2d1} \\
389\bar{\Delta} \bar{\mu} -
390(\bar{\mu} \otimes |)(| \otimes \bar{\Delta })&=& t^{n+1} \xi_2
391\quad {\rm mod}\ t^{n+2} , \\
392\bar{\Delta} \bar{\mu} -
393( | \otimes \bar{\mu})( \bar{\Delta } \otimes | )
394&=& t^{n+1} \xi_2'
395\quad {\rm mod}\ t^{n+2} , \label{hoch2d2}\\
396(\bar{\Delta} \otimes |) \bar{\Delta} - (| \otimes \bar{\Delta})\bar{\Delta}
397&=& t^{n+1} \xi_3
398\quad {\rm mod}\ t^{n+2} . \label{hoch2d3}
399\end{eqnarray*}
400\begin{remark}\label{deformrem}
401{\rm
402The operators in the quadruple $(\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_2', \xi_3)$
403form the {\it primary obstructions}
404to formal deformations of multiplication and comultiplication
405of a Frobenius algebra \cite{MrSt}.
406} \end{remark}
407For the associativity of $\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1} \mu_{n+1}$ mod
408$t^{n+2}$ we obtain:
409$$(\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1} \mu_{n+1})((\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1} \mu_{n+1}) \otimes |)-
410(\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1} \mu_{n+1})(| \otimes (\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1}
411\mu_{n+1}))=0 \ {\rm mod}\ t^{n+2} $$ which is equivalent by
412degree calculations to:
413\begin{eqnarray}
414(d^{2,1}(\mu_{n+1})= ) & & \mu (| \otimes \mu_{n+1})
415+ \mu_{n+1}(| \otimes \mu )
416- \mu (\mu_{n+1} \otimes |)
417-\mu_{n+1}(\mu \otimes |)
418=\xi_1,
419\label{fro2cocy1}
420\end{eqnarray}
421where $d^{2,1}$ is one of the differentials we will define in the following section.
422Similarly, from the Frobenius compatibility condition and
423coassociativity we obtain
424\begin{eqnarray}
425(d^{2,2}_{(1)}(\mu_{n+1}, \Delta_{n+1})= ) & &
426\Delta \mu_{n+1}
427+ \Delta_{n+1} \mu -
428(\mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \Delta_{n+1} )
429- (\mu_{n+1} \otimes |)(| \otimes \Delta )=\xi_2,
430\label{fro2cocy21}\\
431(d^{2,2}_{(2)}(\mu_{n+1}, \Delta_{n+1})= ) & &
432\Delta \mu_{n+1}
433+ \Delta_{n+1} \mu -
434(| \otimes \mu)(\Delta_{n+1} \otimes |)
435- ( | \otimes \mu_{n+1})( \Delta \otimes | )=\xi_2',
436\label{fro2cocy22}\\
437(d^{2,3}(\Delta_{n+1})= ) & &
438(\Delta \otimes |) \Delta_{n+1}
439+ (\Delta_{n+1} \otimes |) \Delta
440- (| \otimes \Delta) \Delta_{n+1}
441- (| \otimes \Delta_{n+1} ) \Delta=
442\xi_3,
443\label{fro2cocy3}
444\end{eqnarray}
445where there are two types of compatibility conditions
446for $d^{2,2}$.
447In summary we proved the following:
448\begin{lemma} \label{deformlem}
449The maps $\bar{\mu}+t^{n+1} \mu_{n+1}$
450and $\bar{\Delta}+t^{n+1} \Delta_{n+1}$ satisfy the
451associativity, coassociativity and
452Frobenius compatibility conditions mod $t^{n+2}$
453if and only if
454the equalities (\ref{fro2cocy1}), (\ref{fro2cocy21}), (\ref{fro2cocy22}) and (\ref{fro2cocy3}) are satisfied.
455\end{lemma}
456\subsection{Chain groups}
457Let $A$ be a Frobenius algebra.
458We define chain groups as follows.
459\begin{eqnarray*}
460C^{n, i}_f (A;A) & =& \Hom(A^{\otimes (n+1-i)}, A^{\otimes i} ), \\
461C^n_f (A;A) & =& \oplus_{ 0 <
462i \leq n} \ C^{n, i}_f (A;A) .
463\end{eqnarray*}
464Specifically, chain groups in low dimensions of our concern are:
465\begin{eqnarray*}
466C^1_f (A;A) &=& \Hom(A, A), \\
467C^2_f (A;A) &=& \Hom(A^{\otimes 2}, A)\oplus \Hom(A, A^{\otimes 2}), \\
468C^3_f (A;A) &=& \Hom(A^{\otimes 3}, A)\oplus
469\Hom(A^{\otimes 2}, A^{\otimes 2})\oplus \Hom(A, A^{\otimes 3}).
470\end{eqnarray*}
471In the remaining sections we will define differentials that are
472homomorphisms between the chain groups:
473$$d^{n, i}_f = d^{n, i}: C^n_f (A;A)
474\rightarrow C^{n+1, i}_f (A;A) (= \Hom(A^{\otimes (n+2-i)}, A^{\otimes i} ) )$$
475which will be defined individually for $n=1,2,3$ and for $i$ with $0 \leq i \leq n$,
476and
477\begin{eqnarray*}
478D_1 & =& d^{1, 1}-d^{1,2} : C^1_f (A;A) \rightarrow C^2_f (A;A) ,\\
479D_2^{(i)}&=& d^{2, 1} + d^{2, 2}_{(i)} + d^{2, 3}: C^2_f (A;A) \rightarrow C^3_f (A;A)
480,\\
481D_3&=& d^{3, 1} +d^{3, 2} +d^{3, 3} +d^{3, 4}:
482C^3_f (A;A) \rightarrow C^4_f (A;A) .
483\end{eqnarray*}
484Define $C^0_f(A;A)=0$ by convention. {}From now on
485the subscripts
486$f$ for differentials are omitted for simplicity if no confusion
487arises.
488\subsection{First differentials}
489By analogy with the differential for associative multiplication, we
490make the following definition:
491\begin{figure}[htb]
492\begin{center}
493\includegraphics[width=5in]{d1}
494\end{center}
495\caption{First differentials }
496\label{d1}
497\end{figure}
498\begin{definition}{\rm
499The first differentials $d^{1,1}: C^{1, 1}_f(A;A) \rightarrow
500C^{2,1}_f (A;A) $ and $d^{1,2}: C^{1, 1}_f(A;A) \rightarrow
501C^{2,2}_f (A;A) $
502are defined, respectively, by
503\begin{eqnarray*}
504d^{1,1}(h) &=& \mu (h \otimes |)+ \mu (| \otimes h) - h\mu , \\
505d^{1,2}(h) &=& (h \otimes |)\Delta + (| \otimes h) \Delta-
506\Delta h .
507\end{eqnarray*}
508Then define $D_1: C^1_f (A;A) \rightarrow C^2_{f} (A;A)$ by
509$D_1=d^{1,1}-d^{1,2}$.
510} \end{definition}
511Diagrammatically, we represent $d^{1,i}$ for $i=1,2$, as depicted in
512Fig.~\ref{d1}. A map $h \in C^{1, 1}_f(A;A)$ is represented by a
513white circle on a vertical string and the multiplication and comultiplication
514are depicted by
515two distinct trivalent vertices as before.
516\subsection{Second Differentials}
517An analogy with deformation theory when $\bar{\mu}=\mu + t \phi_1$
518and $\bar{\Delta}=\Delta + t \phi_2$ gives the following.
519\begin{definition}{\rm
520Define the second differentials by:
521\begin{eqnarray*}
522d^{2,1} (\phi_1 , \phi_2 ) = d^{2,1}(\phi_1) &=& \mu (\phi_1 \otimes |) + \phi_1 (\mu \otimes |)
523- \mu (| \otimes \phi_1)
524- \phi_1 (| \otimes \mu) , \\
525d^{2,2}_{(1)} (\phi_1 , \phi_2) &=& \Delta \phi_1 + \phi_2 \mu
526- (\phi_1 \otimes |)(| \otimes \Delta)
527-
528(\mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \phi_2), \\
529d^{2,2}_{ (2)} (\phi_1 , \phi_2) &=& \Delta \phi_1 + \phi_2 \mu
530- (| \otimes \phi_1)( \Delta \otimes |)
531-
532(| \otimes \mu)( \phi_2 \otimes |), \\
533d^{2,3} (\phi_1 , \phi_2) = d^{2,3}(\phi_2) &=& (\phi_2 \otimes |)\Delta
534+ (\Delta \otimes |) \phi_2
535- (| \otimes \phi_2) \Delta
536- (| \otimes \Delta) \phi_2 .
537\end{eqnarray*}
538} \end{definition} Diagrams for $2$-cochain and $2$-differentials
539are depicted in Fig.~\ref{d21} for $d^{2,1} $ and Fig.~\ref{d22} for $d^{2,2}_{ (1) }$ and $d^{2,2}_{ (2) }$, respectively,
540where $\phi_1 \in C^{2,1}_f(A;A)$ and $\phi_2\in C^{2,2}_f(A;A)$
541are represented by black triangles on two different trivalent vertices.
542The diagrams for $d^{2,3} $ are upside-down pictures of
543Fig.~\ref{d21}.
544\begin{figure}[htb]
545\begin{center}
546\includegraphics[width=3in]{d21}
547\end{center}
548\caption{A $2$-differential $d^{2,1} $}
549\label{d21}
550\end{figure}
551Then define $D_2: C^2_f (A;A) \rightarrow C^2_{f} (A;A)$ by
552$D_2=D_2^{(i)}=d^{2,1}+d^{2,2}_{(i)}+d^{2,3}$ for either
553$i=1$ or $2$.
554Recall that for higher dimensions, differentials depend on this
555choice of $i=1$ or $2$ at this exact dimension $2$ for $d^{2,2}_{
556(1) }$ or $d^{2,2}_{ (2) }$, due to compatibility.
557To avoid duplication in exposition, we choose,
558once and for all, $i=1$. The case for $i=2$ will be clear, as all
559the maps corresponding to $ (\mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \Delta)$ in
560the case $i=1$ are simply replaced by those corresponding to $(|
561\otimes \mu) (\Delta \otimes |)$ in the case $i=2$. Diagrammatically they are mirror images.
562In the case $i=1$, the map looks like the letter ``N''
563and its mirror in the case $i=2$.
564\begin{figure}[htb]
565\begin{center}
566\includegraphics[width=5in]{d22}
567\end{center}
568\caption{$2$-differentials $d^{2,2}_{ (1) }$ and $d^{2,2}_{ (2) }$}
569\label{d22}
570\end{figure}
571\begin{theorem}\label{dd2thm}
572$D_2 D_1=0$.
573\end{theorem}
574{\it Proof.\/}
575This follows from direct calculations and also can be seen from diagrams as depicted in
576Fig.~\ref{dd22}.
577$\Box$
578\begin{figure}[htb]
579\begin{center}
580\includegraphics[width=4in]{dd22}
581\end{center}
582\caption{The $2$-cocycle condition for a $2$-coboundary:
583$d^{2,2}_{ (1) }( d^{1,1}, d^{1,2} )=0$}
584\label{dd22}
585\end{figure}
586{}From the definition of the primary obstruction in Remark~\ref{deformrem},
587the definition of the second differential implies the following.
588\begin{lemma} \label{deform2lem}
589For a deformation $(\bar{\mu}+\mu_{n+1}, \bar{\Delta}+\Delta_{n+1})$
590of the multiplication and comultiplication of
591a Frobenius algebra $A$ defined in Section~\ref{deformsec}
592and the primary obstruction $(\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_2', \xi_3)$ defined in
593Remark~\ref{deformrem},
594the relations $D_2^{(1)}(\mu_{n+1}, \Delta_{n+1})=(\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_3)$
595and $D_2^{(2)}(\mu_{n+1}, \Delta_{n+1})=(\xi_1, \xi_2', \xi_3)$ hold.
596In particular, the primary obstructions vanish
597if and only if
598$(\mu_{n+1}, \Delta_{n+1})$ is a $2$-cocycle.
599\end{lemma}
600\subsection{Third differentials}
601For simplicity we continue to use the case $d^{2,2}_{(1)}$ corresponding to
602$ (\mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \Delta)$
603for higher dimensions, and omit subscripts
604$(1)$ from all the differentials.
605\begin{definition}{\rm
606Define the third differentials by:
607\begin{eqnarray*}
608d^{3,1} (\xi_1 , \xi_2, \xi_3 ) &=& \mu (\xi_1 \otimes |) + \xi_1 (| \otimes \mu \otimes |)
609+ \mu (| \otimes \xi_1)
610- \xi_1 ( \mu \otimes | ) - \xi_1 ( | \otimes \mu) , \\
611d^{3,2}(\xi_1 , \xi_2, \xi_3) &=&
612\Delta \xi_1 + \xi_2 (| \otimes \mu ) + ( \mu \otimes |)(| \otimes \xi_2 )
613-\xi_2 (\mu \otimes | ) - (\xi_1 \otimes |)( |^{\otimes 2} \otimes \Delta ), \\
614d^{3,3}(\xi_1 , \xi_2, \xi_3) &=&
615\xi_3 \mu + (| \otimes \Delta ) \xi_2 + (| \otimes \xi_2 )( \Delta \otimes |)
616- (\Delta \otimes | )\xi_2 -( |^{\otimes 2} \otimes \mu ) (\xi_3 \otimes |), \\
617d^{3,4} (\xi_1 , \xi_2, \xi_3 ) &=&(\xi_3 \otimes |) \Delta + (| \otimes \Delta \otimes |)\xi_3
618+ (| \otimes \xi_3) \Delta
619- \xi_1 ( \mu \otimes | ) - ( | \otimes \Delta)\xi_3 .
620\end{eqnarray*}
621} \end{definition}
622and recall that $$D_3=d^{3, 1} +d^{3, 2} +d^{3,
6233} +d^{3, 4}:
624C^3_f (A;A) \rightarrow C^4_f (A;A).$$
625\begin{figure}[htb]
626\begin{center}
627\includegraphics[width=2.5in]{d32circle}
628\end{center}
629\caption{Deriving a $3$-differential $d^{3,2}$}
630\label{d32circle}
631\end{figure}
632\begin{figure}[htb]
633\begin{center}
634\includegraphics[width=3.5in]{d32}
635\end{center}
636\caption{A $3$-differential $d^{3,2}$}
637\label{d32}
638\end{figure}
639The differentials $d^{3,1}$ and $d^{3,4}$ are the Hochschild differentials
640that are derived from the pentagon conditions for associativity and coassociativity, respectively.
641The differentials $d^{3,2}$ and $d^{3,3}$ are dual in the sense that once one is described via graphs, then the other is a mirror reflection in a horizontal line. We turn to describe the third differential $d^{3,2}$. Recall that the $2$-cocycle conditions for a pair of maps $(\phi_1,\phi_2)$ are obtained by replacing incidences of multiplication and comultiplication by $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ in the associativity, compatibility, and coassociativity conditions. The equalities are depicted as equalities of graphs that contain trivalent vertices. The equalities themselves, then, can be depicted as 4-valent vertices. There are three such vertices: a $(3,1)$ vertex corresponds to associativity (3 up, 1 down), a $(2,2)$ vertex corresponds to either one of the compatibility conditions, and a $(1,3)$ vertex corresponds to coassociativity.
642At the top left of Fig.~\ref{d32circle} a graph is depicted that represents the composition $(\Delta)(\mu)(\mu \otimes |)$. There are two ways of deforming this graph using associativity or the $N$-compatibility condition. These transformations are depicted in the
643figure as
644an
645encircled $(3,1)$ vertex on the right arrow or
646an encircled $(2,2)$
647vertex on the left arrow.
648Such vertices represent $\xi_1$ or $\xi_2$, respectively.
649Continuing around the diagram by choosing a new point
650at which an identity could be applied,
651we obtain a pentagon condition which
652can be derived from the pentagon condition
653on parentheses structures
654that gives the Biedenharn-Elliot identity (see \cite{CFS}, for example).
655Now read clockwise in a cycle around the diagram to write down the $3$-coboundary of the pair $(\xi_1,\xi_2)$; motion against the direction of the arrows results in negative coefficients.
656\begin{figure}[htb]
657\begin{center}
658\includegraphics[width=4in]{assoc42}
659\end{center}
660\caption{Diagrams for $d^{4,2}$}
661\label{assoc42}
662\end{figure}
663The pentagon itself can be labeled by a $(3,2)$-vertex that represents a $4$-cochain $\zeta_2 \in C^{3,2}_f(A;A).$ The corresponding $4$-coboundary is a linear combination of the cells in the Stasheff polyhedron depicted in Fig.~\ref{assoc42} in which the cell corresponding to $\zeta_2$ appears as the bottom pentagon, which is drawn as a trapezoid in the figure.
664\begin{theorem}\label{dd3thm}
665$D_3 D_2=0$.
666\end{theorem}
667{\it Proof.\/} Since $d^{3,1}$ and $d^{3,4}$ are the same as the
668Hochschild differentials of bialgebras, and $d^{3,2}$ and $d^{3,3}$
669are dual to each other, we only consider the case of
670$d^{3,2}[D_2(\phi_1, \phi_2)]=0$.
671This again follows from direct calculations,
672and can also be seen from diagrams as in Fig.~\ref{dd32}. In the
673figure, each term of $d^{3,2}$ is replaced by the terms of
674$D_2(\phi_1, \phi_2)$, and the canceling terms are indicated by
675matching integers at the top-left corners of the diagrams. $\Box$
676\begin{figure}[htb]
677\begin{center}
678\includegraphics[width=4.5in]{dd32}
679\end{center}
680\caption{$D_3 D_2=0$}
681\label{dd32}
682\end{figure}
683{}From point of view of deformation theory, continuing from
684Lemma~\ref{deform2lem}, we obtain the following.
685\begin{lemma} \label{deform3lem}
686The primary obstruction $(\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_3)$ and $(\xi_1, \xi_2',
687\xi_3)$ to a deformation of the multiplication and comultiplication
688of a Frobenius algebra $A$ defined in Remark~\ref{deformrem} give a
689$3$-cocycle: $D_3(\xi_1, \xi_2, \xi_3)=0$, and
690$D_3(\xi_1, \xi_2',
691\xi_3)=0$.
692\end{lemma}
693\subsection{Fourth differentials}
694Recall that two third differentials, $d^{3,1}$ and $d^{3,4},$ are
695the same as the Hochschild
696differentials of bialgebras, and $d^{3,2}$ and $d^{3,3}$ are dual
697to each other.
698In fact, even the latter two have the same
699diagrammatic aspect of being a pentagon. Indeed, the graphs
700involved have two edges pointing upward instead of a single edge.
701Since the same phenomena continues to the fourth differentials, we
702only describe
703the formula for $d^{4,2}$.
704As before, $d^{4,1}$ and $d^{4,5}$ are Hochschild differentials, and $d^{4,4}$ is dual to $d^{4,2}$, and $d^{4,3}$ is a self-dual symmetric version of $d^{4,2}$.
705Thus
706an explicit formula, together with diagrammatic explanations for $d^{4,2},$ would suffice.
707\begin{definition} {\rm
708Define $d^{4,2}$ as follows:
709\begin{eqnarray*}
710d^{4,2}(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, \zeta_3, \zeta_4)
711&=& \Delta \zeta_1
712+ \zeta_2 ( \id \otimes \id \otimes \mu)
713+ (\mu \otimes \id)( \id \otimes \zeta_2) \\
714& & - (\zeta_1 \otimes \id)( \id \otimes \id \otimes \id \otimes \Delta)
715- \zeta_2 ( \mu \otimes \id \otimes \id )
716- \zeta_2 ( \id \otimes \mu \otimes \id) .
717\end{eqnarray*}
718}
719\end{definition}
720Figure~\ref{assoc42} depicts the Stasheff polytope (or associahedron) with vertices, edges, and faces having labels adapted to the current purposes: to formulate the fourth differential.
721The polytope consists of six pentagons and three squares. In the current drawing, four of the pentagons are drawn as trapezoids with their fifth vertex appearing as an interior point on each of the shorter of the parallel edges. The boundary of the planar figure represents one of the three squares in the polytope. The drawing, then, is a distortion of a central projection through this face. The other two squares are in the northwestern and southeastern
722center of the figure while the other two pentagons are in the southwest/northeast corners of the center.
723To each vertex,
724we associate a parenthesization of the five letters $a,b,c,d,e$
725so that the resulting string represents a composition of binary products. Each edge corresponds to a single
726change of parenthesis such as $(ab)c$ to $a(bc)$. Meanwhile, a parenthesis structure can also be represented
727by a tree diagram. For example, $(ab)c$ and $a(bc)$ are represented by the first and third
728terms drawn in the RHS in Fig.~\ref{d21}, respectively, where for the moment you should ignore the black triangles. The pentagons in Fig.~\ref{assoc42} are formed as a cycle of such regroupings. The edges, vertices, and faces
729here
730are indicated by tree diagrams which have two upward pointing branches and four downward pointing roots. To form correspondences between these tree and the groupings of $a,b,c,d,e$ bend the right branches down.
731The pentagon in Fig.~\ref{d32circle} represents a $4$-cochain
732$\zeta_2 \in C^{4,2}(A;A)$, which is also represented by a
733$5$-valent circled vertex with three edges pointing down and two
734up. When a $4$-cochain $\zeta_2$ is identified with a pentagon,
735it is regarded as a homotopy of a path that starts from the three
736edges that are three consecutive arrows of the same direction,
737and sweeps the pentagonal face to the two remaining edge arrows. In
738Fig.~\ref{d32circle}, the three
739starting edges and two terminal edges both start at the top left
740corner of the pentagon and
741end at the bottom center.
742If a homotopy starts from two arrows instead, and sweeps the pentagon and ends at the three arrows,
743then
744it is regarded as the negative of the corresponding cochain, $-\zeta_2$. In Fig.~\ref{assoc42}, there is a unique vertex $v_0$ from which all three arrows point out, which is assigned the parenthesized term $(((ab)c)d)e$.
745The unique vertex $v_1$ into which three arrows point is
746assigned
747$a(b((cd)e))$. There are edge paths that follow the directions of arrows that go
748from $v_0$ to $v_1$.
749Such an edge path $\gamma$ is homotopic to itself through
750pentagonal and square faces (including the ``outside square''
751in Fig.~\ref{assoc42}) of the Stasheff polytope
752sweeping the entire sphere of the polytope.
753By formulating each pentagonal face in terms of the maps represented
754by tree diagrams, we obtain the formula for $d^{4,2}$.
755\begin{theorem}\label{dd4thm}
756$D_4 D_3=0$.
757\end{theorem}
758{\it Sketch of proof.\/} This again
759follows from
760direct calculations
761and can
762also be seen from diagrams in Fig.~\ref{assoc42}. Here we explain
763how we see cancelations on diagrams. In computing $D_4 D_3$, the
764terms in expressions in $D_4$ have their $\zeta$-factors
765systematically replaced by expressions that appear in the edges
766of the boundary of each pentagon, but each edge is labeled by an
767operator involving an $\xi$ as indicated, for example, in
768Fig.~\ref{d32circle}. Since each edge is the boundary of exactly
769two regions in the associahedron, the terms cancel. Note that if
770one of the bounded cells is a square, then there is a corresponding
771identity among those four terms --- commutativity of distant
772tensor operators --- that causes the boundaries to cancel. The
773remaining details are left to the reader. $\Box$
774\begin{remark}{\rm While we have not followed through all the details of such a construction, it seems reasonable to parametrize all the higher differentials in terms of the cells of the higher-dimensional Stasheff polytopes. The coboundaries are parametrized by the boundaries of these cells, and that the square of the differential is trivial will follow from the codimension $1$ boundaries appearing on exactly two faces with opposite orientations. In this way, the cohomology of Frobenius algebras should be defined in all dimensions.}\end{remark}
775\subsection{Cohomology Groups}
776For convenience define
777$C^0_f(A;A)=0$ and $D_0=0: C^0_f(A;A)\rightarrow C^1_f(A;A)$.
778Then Theorems~\ref{dd2thm} and \ref{dd3thm} are summarized as:
779\begin{theorem}
780${\cal C}=(C^n, D_n)_{n=0,1,2,3, 4}$ is a chain complex.
781\end{theorem}
782This enables us to define:
783\begin{definition}{\rm
784The {\it Frobenius $n$-coboundary, cocycle}, and {\it cohomology groups} are defined by:
785\begin{eqnarray*}
786B^{n}_f(A;A) &=& {\rm Image}(D_{n-1}) , \\
787Z^{n}_f(A;A) &=& {\rm Ker}(D_n) , \\
788H^{n}_f(A;A) &=& Z^{n}_f(A;A) / B^{n}_f(A;A)
789\end{eqnarray*}
790for $n=1,2,3, 4$.
791} \end{definition}
792The
793lemma below
794follows from the definitions.
795\begin{lemma} \label{d1lem}
796Let $A$ be a Frobenius algebra
797with $1=1_A=\eta{1_k}$.
798Then:
799\noindent
800{\rm (i) }
801$d^{1,1}(h)(1 \otimes 1) = h(1)$, and
802\noindent {\rm (ii) } $d^{1,1}(h)(1 \otimes x)=d^{1,1}(h)(x \otimes
8031)=h(1)x,\;$
804for any $x \in A$.
805\noindent {\rm (iii) }
806If $\gamma(1)=1 \otimes x + x \otimes 1 $ for some $x \in A$, and $h \in Z^1_f(A;A)$,
807then
808$h(x)=\alpha \cdot 1, $ for some constant $\alpha$ such that $2 \alpha =0 \in k$.
809In
810particular, $h(x)=0$ if $\ch(k)\neq 2$.
811\end{lemma}
812{\it Proof.\/} One computes $d^{1,1}(h)(1 \otimes 1) = h(1)$,
813and
814(ii)
815follows from
816direct calculations.
817For (iii), using $d^{1,2}(h)(1)=0$, we obtain $h(x)\otimes 1 + 1 \otimes h(x)=0$, which
818implies
819the statement.
820$\Box$
821\begin{lemma} \label{d2lem}
822If a Frobenius algebra $A$ is commutative and $d^{2,1}(\phi_1)=0$,
823then for any $x \in A$, the following hold:
824\begin{eqnarray*}
825& & x \phi_1(1\otimes 1)=\phi_1(1\otimes x)=\phi_1(x\otimes 1) , \\
826& & \phi_1(x^2\otimes x)=\phi_1(x\otimes x^2), \quad
827\phi_1(1\otimes x^2)=x \phi_1(1 \otimes x) .
828\end{eqnarray*}
829\end{lemma}
830{\it Proof.\/} One computes $d^{2,1}(\phi_1)(a \otimes b \otimes c) $
831for
832$(a,b,c)=(1,1,x)$ and $ (x,1,1)$,
833for the first set of equations, and
834$(x, x,x)$, $(1,x,x)$ for the second set,
835respectively. The other choices using two elements
836$\{ 1, x \}$ do not give additional conditions. $\Box$
837\subsection{Examples}
838In this subsection we choose $d^{2,2}_{(1)}$ for the chain complex to compute.
839Throughout this section, the symbols $\gamma^{ab}_c$ and $\lambda^{a}_{bc}$ indicate the structure constants of comultiplication and multiplication for the algebras in question.
840\begin{example}\label{cplxcoh}{\rm
841For the example of complex numbers in Example~\ref{cplxex},
842we have
843$$H^1_f (\C;\C) = 0, \quad
844Z^2_f (\C ; \C) = \R^6, \quad
845H^2_f (\C ; \C) = \R^4 .
846$$
847\noindent
848{\it Proof.\/}
849By Lemma~\ref{d1lem} (i), for $h \in Z^1_f (\C; \C)$,
850we have $h(1)=0$, and from
851$d^{1,1}(h)(i \otimes i)=0$, we obtain $h(i)=0$.
852Thus we obtain $Z^1_f(\C; \C)=0=H^1_f (\C;\C) $.
853This also
854implies that
855$B^2_f(\C; \C)
856\cong \R^2$.
857By Lemma~\ref{d2lem}, we have $$ i \phi_1(1\otimes 1)=\phi_1(1\otimes i)=\phi_1(i\otimes 1) $$ from $d^{2,1}(\phi_1)=0$.
858Hence
859we write $$\phi_1(1\otimes i)=\phi_1(i\otimes 1) = \lambda 1 + \lambda' i $$ for some $\lambda, \lambda' \in \R$, and then $ \phi_1(1\otimes 1)= \lambda' 1 - \lambda i $.
860By setting
861$\phi_2(a)=\sum_{b,c} \gamma_a^{b,c} (b \otimes c)$ for basis
862elements $a, b, c \in \{ 1, i\}$, $d^{2,3}(\phi_2)=0$ implies
863\begin{eqnarray}
864\gamma_1^{1,1} = \gamma_i^{1,i}=\gamma_i^{i,1}, & & \label{Ccocy2eq1} \\
865- \gamma_i^{1,1} = \gamma_1^{1,i}=\gamma_1^{i,1}, & & \label{Ccocy2eq2}
866\end{eqnarray}
867leaving free variables $\gamma_1^{1,1}$, $\gamma_1^{i,i}$,
868$\gamma_i^{1,1}$ and $\gamma_i^{i,i}$. The equations
869$d^{2,2}_{(1)}(\phi_1, \phi_2)(1 \otimes 1)=0$ and
870$d^{2,2}_{(1)}(\phi_1, \phi_2)(1 \otimes i)=0$ do not give
871additional conditions. Assuming that $\phi_1(i \otimes
872i)=\lambda_{i,i}^1\;1 + \lambda_{i,i}^i\;i,$
873the other two conditions of $d^{2,2}_{(1)}(\phi_1, \phi_2)=0$
874give
875$$ - \lambda + \lambda_{i,i}^i + \gamma_i^{i,i} - \gamma_1^{1,i}= 0,
876\quad
877\lambda' + \lambda_{i,i}^1 + \gamma_1^{i,i} +\gamma_i^{1,i}=0 ,
878$$
879that
880can be rewritten with Eqns.~(\ref{Ccocy2eq1}) and (\ref{Ccocy2eq2})
881as
882\begin{eqnarray}
883- \lambda + \lambda_{i,i}^i + \gamma_i^{i,i} + \gamma_i^{1,1}&=& 0,
884\label{Ccocy2eq3} \\
885\lambda' + \lambda_{i,i}^1 + \gamma_1^{i,i} +\gamma_1^{1,1}&=&0 .
886\label{Ccocy2eq4}
887\end{eqnarray}
888Since dim$(Z^2_f(A;A))$ is equal to the number of variables $( \lambda, \lambda', \lambda_{i,i}^1, \lambda_{i,i}^i, \gamma_1^{1,1}, \gamma_1^{i,i}, \gamma_i^{1,1}, \gamma_i^{i,i} )$ minus the number of equations (Eqns.~(\ref{Ccocy2eq3}) and (\ref{Ccocy2eq4})), we obtain dim$(Z^2_f(A;A))=6$.
889Hence,
890together with $B^2_f(\C; \C)\cong \R^2$, we obtain the stated results.
891} \end{example}
892\begin{example}\label{polycoh}{\rm
893For $A=k[x]/(x^2)$ in Example~\ref{polyex}, we have
894$$ H^1_f (A;A) = \left\{
895\begin{array}{l} 0 \quad {\rm if } \quad
896\ch(k) \neq 2 \\ k \quad {\rm if } \quad
897\ch(k) = 2
898\end{array} \right. ,
899\quad
900Z^2_f (A; A)
901= k^6 ,
902\quad
903H^2_f (A;A)
904=
905\left\{
906\begin{array}{l} k^4 \quad {\rm if } \quad \ch(k) \neq 2
907\\ k^5 \quad {\rm if } \quad \ch(k) = 2
908\end{array} \right.
909$$
910{\it Proof.\/}
911{}From the proof of Lemma~\ref{d1lem}, the condition
912$h \in Z^1_f(A;A)$ is equivalent to
913$h(1)=0$, $h(x)=\alpha \cdot 1$ with $2 \alpha =0,$ and
914the following additional conditions that were not used in the proof:
915\begin{eqnarray*}
916d^{1,1}(h)(x\otimes x) & = & h(x) \cdot x + x \cdot h(x) - h(0)
917=2xh(x)=0, \\
918d^{1,2}(h)(x)&=& h(x) \otimes x + x \otimes h(x)
919- \Delta (h(x))=0,
920\end{eqnarray*}
921both of which follow from the conditions already stated in the lemma.
922Hence
923we obtain $H^1_f$ as stated.
924We also have
925$B^2(A;A)\cong k^2$ if $\ch(k)\neq 2$ and $B^2(A;A)
926\cong k$ if $\ch(k)=2$.
927For $2$-cocycles $\phi_1 \in C^{2,1}(A;A)$ and
928$\phi_2 \in C^{2,2}(A;A)$, Lemma~\ref{d2lem}
929implies that
930there is $\lambda \in k$ such that $$\phi_1(1 \otimes x)=\phi_1(x \otimes 1)= \lambda x$$
931and $\phi_1(1 \otimes 1)=\lambda 1 + \lambda' x$ for another
932$\lambda' \in k$.
933Direct calculations show also if $\phi_2 (a) = \sum_{b, c} \gamma_a^{b, c} (b \otimes c)$ then $d^{2,3}(\phi_2)=0$
934implies
935$$ \gamma_x^{1,x}= \gamma_x^{x,1}=0, \quad \gamma_1^{1,x}= \gamma_1^{x,1}=\gamma_x^{x,x}.
936$$ Now let
937$\phi_1(x \otimes x)=\alpha 1 +\beta x$.
938The equation $d^{2,2}_{(1)}(\phi_1, \phi_2)(x \otimes 1)=0$
939implies
940$\phi_1(x \otimes x)=\gamma_x^{1,1} 1-\gamma_1^{1,1} x$, (the evaluations at other tensors don't give any extra conditions).
941In summary we
942obtain
943$\phi_2(x)=\gamma_x^{1,1}(1 \otimes 1)+ \gamma_1^{1,x}(x \otimes x)$ and
944$\phi_2(1)= \gamma_1^{1,1} (1 \otimes 1) +\gamma_1^{1,x} ( 1 \otimes x +x \otimes 1) + \gamma_1^{x,x}(x \otimes x )$,
945in total a six-dimensional solution set parametrized by $\lambda, \lambda', \gamma_1^{1,1}, \gamma_x^{1,1},\gamma_1^{1,x}$ and $\gamma_1^{x,x}$.
946The result follows.
947} \end{example}
948\begin{example}\label{gpcoh}{\rm
949For a group algebra $A=kG$ in Example~\ref{gpex},
950we consider the case $G=\Z_2$. Then we have
951$$
952H^1_f (A;A) =
953\left\{
954\begin{array}{l} 0 \quad {\rm if } \quad \ch(k) \neq 2 \\
955k \quad {\rm if } \quad \ch(k) = 2
956\end{array} \right. ,
957\quad
958Z^2_f (A; A)= k^6 ,
959\quad
960H^2_f (A;A)
961=
962\left\{
963\begin{array}{l} k^4 \quad {\rm if } \quad \ch(k) \neq 2 \\
964k^5 \quad {\rm if } \quad \ch(k) = 2
965\end{array} \right.
966$$
967{\it Proof.\/}
968Assuming $d^{1,1}(h)=0$ for
969$h \in C^1_f(A;A)$, Lemma~\ref{d1lem} implies that
970$h(1)=0$.
971The condition $d^{1,1}(h)(x \otimes x)=0$
972implies
973$2xh(x)=0$, which
974is equivalent to
975$2h(x)=0$.
976The same condition
977follows from
978$d^{1,2}(h)(1)=0$,
979and
980the last condition $d^{1,2}(h)(x)=0$
981implies that
982$h(x)=\alpha x $ for some $\alpha \in k$.
983Thus
984we obtain $H^1$ as stated.
985Lemma~\ref{d2lem}
986implies that
987$\phi_1$ is given by $$\phi_1(1\otimes x)=\phi_1(x\otimes 1) = \lambda 1 + \lambda' x $$ for some $\lambda, \lambda' \in k$, and $ \phi_1(1\otimes 1)= \lambda' 1 + \lambda x $.
988{} From $d^{2,3}(\phi_2)=0 $
989we obtain
990$$ \gamma_1^{1,1}=\gamma_x^{1,x}=\gamma_x^{x,1},
991\quad \gamma_x^{1,1}=\gamma_1^{1,x}=\gamma_1^{x,1}.$$
992Hence, we can write
993\begin{eqnarray*}
994\phi_2(1)
995&=& q (1 \otimes 1) + r (1 \otimes x + x \otimes 1)+ \gamma_1^{x,x}(x \otimes x)
996,\\
997\phi_2(x)
998&=& r(1 \otimes 1) + q (1 \otimes x + x \otimes 1) + \gamma_x^{x,x} (x \otimes x).
999\end{eqnarray*}
1000Now let $\phi_1(x \otimes x)=\lambda^1_{x,x}\;1+ \lambda^x_{x,x}\;x$.
1001The equation $d^{2,2}(\phi_1, \phi_2)=0 $
1002gives by evaluation at the four basis elements the following constraints
1003\begin{eqnarray}
1004\gamma_1^{x,x}+ \lambda_{x,x}^1 &=& q + \lambda' , \label{z2eqn1} \\
1005\gamma_x^{x,x}- \lambda_{x,x}^x &=& r - \lambda . \label{z2eqn2}
1006\end{eqnarray}
1007Since dim$(Z^2_f(A;A))$ is equal to the number of variables $(q,r,
1008\lambda, \lambda ', \gamma_1^{x,x}, \gamma_x^{x,x},
1009\lambda_{x,x}^1, \lambda_{x,x}^x$)
1010minus the number of equations
1011(the above two), we obtain dim$(Z^2_f(A;A))=6$. Thus we obtain the
1012result.
1013}\end{example}
1014\begin{remark}{\rm It is interesting that these Frobenius algebras all have the same $1$ and $2$-dimensional cohomology when char($k$)$\ne2$.
1015Nevertheless, the free variables are quite a bit different in each computation. We expect that higher-dimensional algebras are cohomologically distinct.}
1016\end{remark}
1017\section{Yang-Baxter solutions in Frobenius algebras and their cocycle deformations}\label{YBEsec}
1018In this section, we construct YBE solutions ($R$-matrices)
1019from skein theoretic methods using maps in Frobenius algebras.
1020We start with the following examples, the first of which is due to
1021\cite{Stolin}, and diagrammatic proofs are depicted in
1022Figs.~\ref{YBE1}, \ref{AmidaYBE}, and \ref{KYBE}, respectively.
1023The Yang-Baxter equation (YBE) is formulated as $(R \otimes
1024\id)(\id \otimes R)(R \otimes \id) =(\id \otimes R)(R \otimes
1025\id)(\id \otimes R)$ for $R \in {\rm Hom}(V \otimes V, V \otimes
1026V)$, see, for example, \cite{K&P}. It is often required that $R$
1027be invertible, but we do not always require the invertibility
1028unless explicitly mentioned. In particular, the solutions in
1029Lemma~\ref{ybe1lem} are not invertible. Invertible solutions
1030derived from these are discussed in Proposition~\ref{skeinprop}.
1031\begin{lemma}\label{ybe1lem}
1032For any Frobenius algebra $X$,
1033$R=\Delta \mu$ is a solution
1034to the Yang-Baxter equation.
1035For any symmetric Frobenius algebra $X$,
1036$R_1=\tau \Delta \mu$ and
1037$R_2 =(\mu \otimes \id )( \id \otimes \tau) (\Delta \otimes \id)$
1038are solutions
1039to the YBE as well.
1040\end{lemma}
1041\begin{figure}[htb]
1042\begin{center}
1043\includegraphics[width=3in]{YBE1}
1044\end{center}
1045\caption{A solution to YBE in Frobenius algebras}
1046\label{YBE1}
1047\end{figure}
1048\begin{figure}[htb]
1049\begin{center}
1050\includegraphics[width=3.5in]{AmidaYBE}
1051\end{center}
1052\caption{A solution to YBE in symmetric Frobenius algebras}
1053\label{AmidaYBE}
1054\end{figure}
1055\begin{figure}[htb]
1056\begin{center}
1057\includegraphics[width=4in]{KYBE}
1058\end{center}
1059\caption{Another solution to YBE in symmetric Frobenius algebras}
1060\label{KYBE}
1061\end{figure}
1062\begin{example}{\rm
1063For a group ring $X=kG$ in Example~\ref{gpex},
1064the $R$-matrix of type $\Delta \mu$ is
1065computed by $R(x \otimes y) = (\Delta \mu) (x \otimes y)=
1066\sum_{zw=xy}z \otimes w$
1067for $x, y \in G$.
1068} \end{example}
1069\begin{figure}[htb]
1070\begin{center}
1071\includegraphics[width=3in]{skein}
1072\end{center}
1073\caption{A skein relation}
1074\label{skein}
1075\end{figure}
1076We define
1077two $R$-matrices $R$ and $R'$
1078by
1079skein relations as depicted in Fig.~\ref{skein},
1080which are written as follows.
1081\begin{eqnarray}
1082R & = & A \id^{\otimes 2} + B ( \gamma \beta ) + C (\Delta \mu) + T(\tau), \label{skein1}\\
1083R' &=& A' \id^{\otimes 2} + B' (\gamma \beta ) + C' (\Delta \mu)+ T'(\tau). \label{skein2}
1084\end{eqnarray}
1085We call this the {\it Frobenius skein relation},
1086and below we derive conditions for it to satisfy the YBE.
1087We also suppose that the inverse of $R$ is
1088given by $R'$, and compute the conditions for this requirement.
1089Note that instead of the map $ \Delta \mu$,
1090the two other solutions in Lemma~\ref{ybe1lem}
1091can be used to define similar skein relations, and
1092these possibilities might deserve further study.
1093Note that
1094$\beta \gamma (1)$ is an element of $k$ which we denote by $\delta_0$.
1095In the following, sometimes we make the assumption that
1096$\mu \Delta = \delta_1 {\rm \id}$
1097for some $\delta_1 \in k$
1098for computational simplicity.
1099(Recall that in general it is true that
1100$\mu \Delta = \delta_h {\rm \id}$
1101holds but $\delta_h \in A$
1102is a central element.)
1103This holds for some of the examples
1104of Frobenius algebras, such as
1105group algebras.
1106Under this assumption one obtains
1107the following relation:
1108\begin{eqnarray}
1109\delta_0 = \beta \gamma= \epsilon \mu \Delta \eta (1)
1110=\epsilon (\delta_1 1 ) = \delta_1 \epsilon (1). \label{delta0eq}
1111\end{eqnarray}
1112\begin{figure}[htb]
1113\begin{center}
1114\includegraphics[width=5in]{bubble2}
1115\end{center}
1116\caption{A few formulas}
1117\label{bubble2}
1118\end{figure}
1119\begin{figure}[htb]
1120\begin{center}
1121\includegraphics[width=4.5in]{skeininv}
1122\end{center}
1123\caption{The skein relation of the inverse}
1124\label{skeininv}
1125\end{figure}
1126In Fig.~\ref{bubble2} a few direct calculations are depicted that will be used below.
1127Using
1128this notation, one calculates the condition
1129for $R'$ to be the inverse of $R$.
1130A calculation is illustrated in Fig.~\ref{skeininv} for
1131the condition that $R'=R^{-1}$.
1132In Figs.~\ref{skeinL} and \ref{skeinR}
1133the YBE is formulated diagrammatically for the above defined skein relation.
1134\begin{figure}[htb]
1135\begin{center}
1136\includegraphics[width=5.5in]{skeinL}
1137\end{center}
1138\caption{YBE for a skein, LHS}
1139\label{skeinL}
1140\end{figure}
1141\begin{figure}[htb]
1142\begin{center}
1143\includegraphics[width=5.5in]{skeinR}
1144\end{center}
1145\caption{YBE for a skein, RHS}
1146\label{skeinR}
1147\end{figure}
1148\begin{proposition}\label{skeinprop}
1149Suppose
1150the Frobenius algebra $X$ over a field $k$
1151satisfies $\mu \Delta = \delta_1 {\id}$
1152for some $\delta_1 \in k$.
1153Then the
1154$R$-matrix defined by the Frobenius skein relation~(\ref{skein1}),
1155with the inverse $R^{-1}=R'$ defined by the relation~(\ref{skein2}),
1156gives a solution to the YBE if
1157the following
1158hold:
1159\noindent
1160{\rm (i)}
1161$C=T=0$, $C'=T'=0$,
1162$A^2 + B^2 + \delta_0 AB=0$,
1163$A'^2 + B'^2 + \delta_0 A'B'=0$,
1164and $A B'+A'B+\delta_0 BB'=0$.
1165\noindent
1166{\rm (ii)}
1167$X$ is commutative,
1168$A=B=0$, $A'=B'=0$, $TT'=1$ and $CT'+C'T+ \delta_1 CC'=0$.
1169\end{proposition}
1170{\it Proof.\/}
1171We obtain the conditions
1172$A^2 T=0$ and $B^2 T=0$
1173by comparing the coefficients of the following terms for both sides of the equation
1174respectively (see Figs.~\ref{skeinL} and \ref{skeinR}):
1175\begin{eqnarray*}
1176& &\id \otimes \tau , \ \tau \otimes \id , \\
1177& &(\id \otimes \tau)(\gamma \otimes \id)(\beta \otimes \id),
1178\ (\tau \otimes \id)( \id \otimes \gamma)( \id \otimes \beta) ,
1179\ (\beta \otimes \id)(\gamma \otimes \id)(\id \otimes \tau),
1180\ ( \id \otimes \beta)( \id \otimes \gamma)(\id \otimes \tau) .
1181\end{eqnarray*}
1182Assuming that variables take values in the field $k$, we obtain
1183either $T=0$ or $A=B=0$.
1184Assume $T=0$, and
1185also assume that $R^{-1}$ satisfies the similar condition, $T'=0$.
1186For $R$ we obtain
1187\begin{eqnarray}
1188B( A^2 + B^2 + \delta_0 AB + \delta_1 BC + 2 \delta_1 A C ) &=&0, \label{skeineq1} \\
1189AC( A + \delta_1 C ) &=&0, \label{skeineq2} \\
1190BC( B + \delta_1 C ) &=&0, \label{skeineq3}
1191\end{eqnarray}
1192that are derived from comparing the coefficients of the
1193following maps:
1194\begin{eqnarray*}
1195& &\id \otimes \gamma \beta, \ \gamma \beta \otimes \id , \\
1196& &(\id \otimes \Delta \mu) , \ (\Delta \mu \otimes \id) , \\
1197& &(\id \otimes \gamma)\mu (\mu \otimes \id) ,
1198\ ( \gamma \otimes \id )\mu (\mu \otimes \id) ,
1199\ (\Delta \otimes \id)\Delta (\id \otimes \beta),
1200\ (\id \otimes \Delta )\Delta (\beta \otimes \id ) .
1201\end{eqnarray*}
1202It is, then, easy to see from these equations and from
1203Figs.~\ref{skeinL} and \ref{skeinR}
1204that the conditions
1205$C=T=0$ and $A^2 + B^2 + \delta_0 AB=0$
1206give solution $R$ to the YBE. Similarly from the condition
1207depicted in Fig.~\ref{skeininv},
1208it follows that $R'$ gives the inverse of $R$ with the conditions
1209$C'=T'=0$, $A'^2 + B'^2 + \delta_0 A'B'=0$
1210and $A B'+A'B+\delta_0 BB'=0$.
1211In this paragraph we observe that the condition $C=0$, in fact,
1212follows from
1213the required conditions assuming that variables take values in a field $k$.
1214Suppose $C\neq 0$.
1215Then Eqns. (\ref{skeineq2}) and (\ref{skeineq3})
1216require $A=B=-\delta_1 C $ and $A'=B'=-\delta_1 C' $.
1217Then Eqn.
1218(\ref{skeineq1})
1219implies
1220$\delta_0=1$, and from Eqn.
1221(\ref{delta0eq}) ($\delta_0=\delta_1 \epsilon(1)$),
1222we have $\delta_1=\epsilon(1)^{-1}$.
1223The inverse formula (Fig.~\ref{skeininv}) in this case ($C=T=0$) requires $A B'+A'B+\delta_0 BB'=0$, which reduces to $\delta_1CC'=0$, a contradiction.
1224Hence
1225we have $C=0$.
1226Next we consider the case
1227$A=B=0$, and assume that $R^{-1}$ is in the same form, $A'=B'=0$.
1228Then the commutativity
1229implies
1230LHS$=$RHS in Figs.~\ref{skeinL}
1231and \ref{skeinR},
1232using formulas depicted in Fig.~\ref{bubble2}.
1233The inverse condition in
1234Fig.~\ref{skeininv} and the definition $R^{-1}=C'(\Delta \mu )+ T' \tau$
1235imply $TT'= 1$ and
1236$CT'+C'T+\delta_1 CC'=0$.
1237This leads to Case (ii).
1238$\Box$
1239\bigskip
1240Using $2$-cocycles,
1241we construct new $R$-matrices from old by deformation
1242as follows.
1243Let $X$ be a Frobenius algebra over $k$.
1244Suppose $R$ is defined by the Frobenius skein relation
1245that satisfies the conditions in Proposition~\ref{skeinprop},
1246so that $R$ is a solution to the YBE on $X$.
1247Let $\hat{X}=A \otimes k[[t]] / (t^2)$.
1248Then $\hat{X}$ is regarded as $ (k[t]/ (t^2) )$-module.
1249Extend the maps $\mu$ and $\Delta$ to $\hat{X}$.
1250{}From the
1251deformation interpretation of $2$-cocycles in Section~\ref{deformsec},
1252we have the following.
1253\begin{theorem}\label{deformRthm}
1254Let $X$ be a commutative, and therefore cocommutative, Frobenius algebra.
1255Suppose $\phi_i \in C^{2}(X;X)$, $i=1,2$,
1256are Frobenius $2$-cochains satisfying all the
1257$2$-cocycle conditions
1258$d^{2,1} = d^{2,2}_{(1)} =d^{2,2}_{(2)}=d^{2,3} =0$.
1259Define $R_{\phi_1, \phi_2} : \hat{X} \otimes \hat{X} \rightarrow \hat{X} \otimes \hat{ X} $
1260by
1261$$R_{\phi_1, \phi_2}=
1262C ( (\Delta+ t \phi_2)( \mu + t \phi_1)) + T(\tau). $$
1263Then
1264$R_{\phi_1, \phi_2}$ is a solution to the YBE if the following conditions are satisfied:
1265$(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)=\delta_1 \id$ on $ \hat{X}$
1266for some $\delta_1 \in k[t]/ (t^2)$,
1267$\phi_1 \tau=\phi_1$, and $\tau \phi_2 = \phi_2$.
1268\end{theorem}
1269{\it Proof.\/} This is a repetition of the proof of
1270Proposition~\ref{skeinprop}
1271Case (ii), using the deformation interpretations
1272of $2$-cocycle conditions. The associativity, coassociativity, and
1273Frobenius compatibility conditions for $\mu + t \phi_1$ and $\Delta +
1274t \phi_2$ follow from the $2$-cocycle conditions in
1275Lemma~\ref{deformlem}. The conditions
1276$\phi_1 \tau=\phi_1$ and $\tau \phi_2 = \phi_2$
1277correspond to the commutativity. $\Box$
1278\begin{example} \label{cplxRex}
1279{\rm
1280For $X=\C$ in Example~\ref{cplxex},
1281the general solutions for the $2$-cocycles $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$
1282with $d^{2,1} = d^{2,2}_{(1)} =d^{2,2}_{(2)}=d^{2,3} =0$ found in
1283Example~\ref{cplxcoh} satisfy the condition (ii)
1284in Theorem~\ref{deformRthm}: $\phi_1 \tau=\phi_1$, $\tau \phi_2 = \phi_2$.
1285We check the condition
1286$(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)=\delta_1 \id$ on $ \hat{X}$
1287for some $\delta_1 \in k[t]/ (t^2)$.
1288One computes:
1289\begin{eqnarray*}
1290(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)(1)&=&
12912+ t\ [ \ (\gamma_1^{1,1} - \gamma_1^{i,i} + \lambda' -\lambda_{i,i}^1)
1292+ ( \gamma_1^{1,i} + \gamma_1^{i,1} - \lambda -\lambda_{i,i}^i) i \ ] , \\
1293(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)(i)&=&
12942i+ t\ [ \ (\gamma_i^{1,1} - \gamma_i^{i,i} +2 \lambda )
1295+ ( \gamma_i^{1,i} + \gamma_i^{i,1} + 2 \lambda' ) i \ ] .
1296\end{eqnarray*}
1297Thus the general $2$-cocycles satisfy $(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)=\delta_1 \id$
1298if and only if
1299the above two values are multiples of $1$
1300and $i$, respectively, by the same element $\delta_1 \in k[t]/ (t^2)$.
1301This condition is written as
1302\begin{eqnarray}
1303\gamma_1^{1,i} + \gamma_1^{i,1} - \lambda -\lambda_{i,i}^i &=& 0 ,\label{CR1}\\
1304\gamma_i^{1,1} - \gamma_i^{i,i} +2 \lambda &=& 0 ,\label{CR2} \\
1305\gamma_1^{1,1} - \gamma_1^{i,i} + \lambda' -\lambda_{i,i}^1
1306&=& \gamma_i^{1,i} + \gamma_i^{i,1} + 2 \lambda' . \label{CR3}
1307\end{eqnarray}
1308For Eqn.~(\ref{CR3}), Eqns.~(\ref{Ccocy2eq1}) and (\ref{Ccocy2eq4}) imply $$ \gamma_1^{1,1} - \gamma_1^{i,i} + \lambda' -\lambda_{i,i}^1= -2 (\gamma_1^{i,i} + \lambda_{i,i}^1) = \gamma_i^{1,i} + \gamma_i^{i,1} + 2 \lambda' , $$ so that Eqn.~(\ref{CR3}) is redundant and we obtain $\delta_1=2[ 1 - t ( \lambda_{i,i}^1+\gamma_1^{i,i} ) ]$.
1309Thus,
1310from the computation in Example~\ref{cplxcoh}, the general $2$-cocycle satisfying the conditions in Theorem~\ref{deformRthm} Case (ii) has variables $( \lambda, \lambda', \lambda_{i,i}^1, \lambda_{i,i}^i, \gamma_1^{1,1}, \gamma_1^{i,i}, \gamma_i^{1,1}, \gamma_i^{i,i} )$, with Eqns.
1311(\ref{Ccocy2eq3}), (\ref{Ccocy2eq4}), (\ref{CR1}),
1312and (\ref{CR2}).
1313Equations (\ref{CR1}) and (\ref{CR2}) reduce with Eqn.~(\ref{Ccocy2eq3})
1314to the same equation
1315\begin{eqnarray}
13163 \gamma_i^{1,1} + 2 \lambda_{i,i}^i + \gamma_i^{i,i}=0, \label{CR4}
1317\end{eqnarray}
1318so the deformed $R$ matrix in this case has $5$ free variables.
1319} \end{example}
1320\begin{example} \label{gpRex}
1321{\rm
1322For $X=k\Z_2$ in Example~\ref{gpex},
1323the general solutions for the $2$-cocycles $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$
1324with $d^{2,1} = d^{2,2}_{(1)} =d^{2,2}_{(2)}=d^{2,3} =0$ found in
1325Example~\ref{gpcoh} satisfy the condition (ii)
1326in Theorem~\ref{deformRthm}: $\phi_1 \tau=\phi_1$, $\tau \phi_2 = \phi_2$.
1327We check the condition
1328$(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)=\delta_1 \id$ on $ \hat{X}$
1329for some $\delta_1 \in k[t]/ (t^2)$.
1330One computes:
1331\begin{eqnarray*}
1332(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)(1)&=& 2+ t\ [ \ (q+
1333\gamma_1^{x,x} + \lambda' +\lambda_{x,x}^1) + ( 2r + \lambda +\lambda_{x,x}^x) x \ ] ,
1334\\ (\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)(x)&=&
13352x+ t\ [ \ (r +\gamma_x^{x,x} +2 \lambda )
1336+ ( 2q + 2 \lambda' ) x \ ] . \end{eqnarray*}
1337Thus the general $2$-cocycles satisfy $(\mu+t \phi_1)(\Delta + t \phi_2)=\delta_1 \id$,
1338if and only if
1339the above two values are multiples of $1$
1340and $x$, respectively by the same element $\delta_1 \in k[t]/ (t^2)$.
1341This condition is written as
1342\begin{eqnarray*}
13432r + \lambda +\lambda_{x,x}^x &=& 0 ,\\
1344r + \gamma_x^{x,x} +2 \lambda &=& 0 ,\\
1345\gamma_1^{x,x} + \lambda' +\lambda_{x,x}^1 &=& q + 2 \lambda' .
1346\end{eqnarray*}
1347Using Eqns.~(\ref{z2eqn1}) and (\ref{z2eqn2}), one obtains
1348$ \lambda^x_{x,x}=3\lambda +2\gamma_x^{x,x}$ and one can compute
1349$\delta_1=2[ 1 + t (\lambda^1_{x,x}+ \gamma_1^{x,x}) ]$. Since the equations listed for Example~\ref{gpcoh} are the only
1350equations we need for this example as well, the deformed $R$ matrix
1351has $5$
1352free variables. }\end{example}
1353\section{Conclusion}
1354This paper contains a study of the cohomology of Frobenius algebras initiated from the point of view of deformation theory as explicated by diagrammatic techniques. One reason for developing this theory diagrammatically is that we
1355obtain cocycle deformations of $R$-matrices,
1356and
1357anticipate topological applications.
1358Several problems remain. Clearly computations of cohomology for
1359Frobenius algebras formed as matrix algebras would be especially
1360interesting if these could be done in a fashion that encompassed
1361all dimensions. The relationship
1362between this Frobenius cohomology theory and the
1363cohomology of the adjoint map in a Hopf algebra deserves study.
1364Finally, an understanding of the possible knot invariants defined
1365by YBE solutions defined by skein relations among maps in
1366Frobenius algebras would be very interesting.
